query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy that is initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state, localized thermal activation during service (or controlled aging) promotes Mg partitioning and the nucleation of Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates—primarily along grain boundaries. The kinetics of this transformation, governed by sluggish diffusion inherent to the high configurational entropy state, determine whether a fine, coherent dispersion of these precipitates forms (thereby retaining protective oxidation and corrosion behavior by supporting a continuous, adherent oxide scale) or whether coarse, incoherent intermetallics develop (which disrupt the continuity of protective oxide layers and cause degradation in high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance).
generation.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a metastable, single-phase solid solution with minimal intermetallic precipitates
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled thermal aging at service-relevant temperatures (e.g., 600–900 °C) for varying durations
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature exposure in atmospheres that simulate high-temperature oxidation and corrosive service environments
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of Mg‐rich intermetallic phases at grain boundaries
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated local solute partitioning of Mg from the metastable solid solution leads to precipitation; the transformation pathway and kinetics (controlled by the intrinsically slow diffusion in HEAs) dictate whether the precipitates remain fine and coherent (supporting the formation of protective oxide scales) or coarsen into incoherent phases that disrupt corrosion/oxidation barriers
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exhibiting a fine, coherent dispersion of Mg‐rich intermetallics will maintain or even enhance corrosion and oxidation resistance compared to the initial state, whereas samples showing coarse intermetallic formation (or significant intermetallic coarsening) will suffer from degradation in these properties
generation.baseline: The as-cast (or as-processed) metastable solid-solution state with negligible intermetallic compound formation and an initially high oxidation/corrosion resistance
generation.boundary: Service conditions defined by temperatures between approximately 600–900 °C and corrosive/oxidative atmospheres, where the transformation kinetics become significant
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical temperature and time scales at which the transformation pathway shifts from beneficial fine-precipitation to deleterious coarse intermetallic formation are not fully constrained; in addition, the role of Mg in modifying the protective oxide composition remains to be quantitatively established

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical sets of the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples; subject one set to controlled thermal aging treatments at incremental temperatures (600, 750, and 900 °C) for various durations, while maintaining a reference set in the as-cast metastable state. Characterize the evolved microstructure (using TEM/SEM with EDS and XRD) to quantify the precipitate size, distribution, and coherence, and correlate these with measured corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance (via standardized weight-gain oxidation tests and electrochemical corrosion tests).
measurements: Microstructural imaging and precipitate size/distribution (TEM/SEM with EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging does not lead to a significant change in the intermetallic precipitate size, distribution or coherence, or if changes in intermetallic morphology do not correlate with a measurable difference in oxidation and corrosion resistance relative to the baseline state, then the proposed mechanism (that Mg partitioning and precipitation control the protective behaviors) is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

In this paper, the impact of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) on the phase evolution and mechanical properties development of CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated. The microstructure and properties of the material were examined, using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology observation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and hardness testing to evaluate mechanical performance. The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases. Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa. Abstract Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. Here, an unexpected ductile–brittle–ductile transition is discovered in a multiphase high‐entropy alloy (HEA) aged in an intermediate temperature regime. Unlike the classical thermal embrittlement driven by grain boundary effects, this transition originates from the dynamic evolution of local chemical order (LCO) and phase boundary (PB) configurations in HEAs. Aging within the embrittlement‐prone regime enhances chemical ordering, increases the density of ordered domains, and induces jagged PBs, collectively triggering plastic instability and the ductile−to−brittle transition. In contrast, aging outside this regime suppresses excessive ordering and promotes the formation of ductile interphase transition zones, facilitating a brittle−to−ductile recovery. The findings offer new insights into the thermal behavior of HEAs and challenge the established paradigm of thermal embrittlement.
